In the October 2017 decision *[Garza v. Hargan](/wiki/Azar_v._Garza "Azar v. Garza")*, Kavanaugh joined an unsigned, divided panel of the District of Columbia Circuit in holding that the [Office of Refugee Resettlement](/wiki/Office_of_Refugee_Resettlement "Office of Refugee Resettlement") does not violate an unaccompanied alien minor's constitutional right to an abortion by requiring that she first be appointed a sponsor before traveling to obtain the abortion, provided "the process of securing a sponsor to whom the minor is released occurs expeditiously".[[79]](#cite_note-79)[[80]](#cite_note-Harv2018-80) Days later, the *[en banc](/wiki/En_banc "En banc")* District of Columbia Circuit reversed that judgment, with Kavanaugh dissenting.[[80]](#cite_note-Harv2018-80)[[81]](#cite_note-81) In his dissent, he criticized the majority for creating "a new right for unlawful immigrant minors in United States government detention to obtain immediate abortion on demand".[[82]](#cite_note-82) The girl then obtained an abortion.[[80]](#cite_note-Harv2018-80) In 2018, in a follow-up petition from the [Solicitor General of the United States](/wiki/Solicitor_General_of_the_United_States "Solicitor General of the United States"), the United States Supreme Court [vacated](/wiki/Vacated_judgment "Vacated judgment") the *en banc* District of Columbia Circuit's judgment and the girl's claim was ultimately dismissed as [moot](/wiki/Mootness "Mootness") and does not serve as precedent.[[83]](#cite_note-83)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/db/BankUnited_Center.JPG/250px-BankUnited_Center.JPG)](/wiki/File:BankUnited_Center.JPG)

[Watsco Center](/wiki/Watsco_Center "Watsco Center") on the [University of Miami](/wiki/University_of_Miami "University of Miami") campus, the home arena of the Hurricanes' [men's](/wiki/Miami_Hurricanes_men%27s_basketball "Miami Hurricanes men's basketball") and [women's](/wiki/Miami_Hurricanes_women%27s_basketball "Miami Hurricanes women's basketball") basketball teams

The [University of Miami](/wiki/University_of_Miami "University of Miami")'s men's basketball team has produced several players who have gone on to play professionally in the [NBA](/wiki/National_Basketball_Association "National Basketball Association"). [Rick Barry](/wiki/Rick_Barry "Rick Barry"), who played his collegiate basketball at the University of Miami, is a member of the [Basketball Hall of Fame](/wiki/Basketball_Hall_of_Fame "Basketball Hall of Fame"). Barry is the Hurricanes' only consensus All-American in basketball and led the nation in scoring his senior year with a 37.4 average during the 1964–65 season.

The University of Miami men's basketball team was launched in 1926. In the middle of the 1970 season, the university's board of trustees attempted to shut the program down, which forced [Will Allen](/wiki/Will_Allen_(urban_farmer) "Will Allen (urban farmer)") to organize his teammates and strike because it was not sufficient notice for the players to transfer schools. They held a press conference, which caught the attention of national media. In 1971, the university dropped the program,[[9]](#cite_note-Biography_Today-9) with the board citing inadequate facilities, sagging attendance, and serious financial losses as justification
